name: Midland ER310
amazon: Midland ER310 emergency crank weather radio
description: An AM/FM/NOAA weather alert radio with crank, solar, a rechargeable pack and a six-AA backup, rated for up to 45 hours; the first radio to put in a home storm kit.
quick: AM/FM/NOAA alert radio with crank, solar, Li-ion pack and AA backup. An AM/FM/NOAA weather alert radio with crank, solar, a rechargeable pack and a six-AA backup, rated for up to 45 hours; the first radio to put in a home storm kit.
bestFor: A home storm kit that needs automatic weather alerts and a disposable-battery backup
skipIf: You mainly want a radio that charges your phone
specs: NOAA weather radio with automatic alert
Hand crank, solar, rechargeable Li-ion, 6 × AA backup

USB output; Midland warns newer phones may not charge
verdict: The Midland ER310 is the radio to put in a household storm kit first. It combines a real NOAA weather alert with four power sources, including AA batteries that work when everything else is gone.

**The alert is the reason to buy it.** It covers AM, FM and NOAA weather radio, and with the alert switched on it sounds a siren when a warning is broadcast on your local channel. That is the feature that wakes you for a 3 a.m. tornado warning. It cannot filter alerts by county, so you will also hear the weekly test.

**Four ways to power it.** It runs from a rechargeable lithium-ion pack, the hand crank, the solar panel and six AA batteries as a backup. The AA option sets it apart, because store-bought batteries are the one source that works on day ten with no sun. Midland rates it for up to 45 hours of normal use. Midland's own pages list the battery as both 3,500mAh and 2,600mAh, so treat the exact capacity as unsettled.

**Honest about phone charging.** Midland's FAQ says the radio will not reliably charge newer iPhones and Android phones, and that solar alone will not revive a dead battery. Buy it for alerts, light and radio; for phones, a bank like the [Anker PowerCore 10000](/gear/anker-powercore-10000/) does far better. The Cree LED flashlight includes an SOS beacon, and an ultrasonic dog whistle is a bonus for finding a pet.

Owners praise the alert, the long runtime and the AA backup. The main complaint is the crank, which takes a lot of turning for a little power. It is the top pick in our [best hand crank radio](/best-hand-crank-radio/) roundup; for a smaller Midland, see the [ER210](/gear/midland-er210/).

faqs.q: Does the Midland ER310 sound an alarm for weather warnings?
faqs.a: Yes. With the weather alert switched on, it monitors your local NOAA weather radio channel and sounds a siren when a warning is broadcast. It cannot filter alerts by county, so you will also hear the weekly test and some warnings for nearby areas. Keep the pack charged through storm season so it can monitor overnight.

faqs.q: What is the difference between the Midland ER310 and the ER210?
faqs.a: Size, runtime and backup power. Both have NOAA weather alerts, a crank, solar charging and a Cree flashlight. The ER310 is larger, rated for up to 45 hours of normal use, and takes six AA batteries as a backup. The ER210 is pocket-sized, rated for up to 25 hours, with no AA backup. For a home kit, pick the ER310.

verdict: The Eton FRX3+ is the compact alert radio for a go-bag or a second room. It packs the important features of the Midland ER310 into a smaller, lighter body.

**Alerts in a small package.** It receives all seven NOAA weather bands with an alert function, plus AM and FM. With the alert on, it sounds when a warning is broadcast on your local channel, the feature that matters most in tornado and hurricane country. Retail listings put it at about 15 oz, light enough for a go-bag.

**Backup power that does not depend on the pack.** The internal lithium pack, which Eton's manual lists as 2,600mAh at 3.7V (about 9.6Wh), recharges by hand crank, by the small solar panel on top or over USB. A AAA battery compartment gives a backup that works even when the pack is flat, a feature the [Midland ER210](/gear/midland-er210/) lacks.

**Light designed for outages.** You get an LED flashlight, a red flashing beacon for signaling and a glow-in-the-dark locator, so you can find the radio in a dark room. A USB output can top up a phone, but 9.6Wh is a partial charge at best, so keep a separate bank like the [Anker PowerCore 10000](/gear/anker-powercore-10000/) for phones.

Owners like the size, the alert and the beacon. The main complaint is the small solar panel, which reviewers describe as slow. Some retailers have listed the FRX3+ as discontinued, so check stock before you count on it. It is the compact pick in our [best hand crank radio](/best-hand-crank-radio/) roundup; for a larger home radio, see the [Midland ER310](/gear/midland-er310/).

verdict: The Midland ER210 takes the core of the ER310 and shrinks it into a radio that fits a glovebox. You keep the weather alert and the bright flashlight, and give up the AA backup.

**The alert in a small body.** You get AM, FM and NOAA weather radio with an automatic alert that sounds when a warning is issued on your local channel. Midland says the siren runs for eight seconds and can be silenced by holding the weather button. At 6.5 × 2.8 × 1.9 inches, it fits a car kit or a go-bag.

**Power, and what is missing.** A rechargeable lithium-ion pack, which Midland lists as 2,600mAh, recharges by crank, by solar or over USB. Midland rates it for up to 25 hours of normal use, a little over half the ER310's 45. The big difference is backup: there is no AA or AAA compartment, so once the pack is empty you are cranking or waiting for sun. Midland's FAQ is candid that solar extends the charge but will not fully charge the radio.

**A real flashlight.** The Cree LED is rated at 130 lumens with an SOS beacon, bright enough to move around a dark house. Midland also warns that many newer phones may not charge from the radio, so keep a bank like the [Anker PowerCore 10000](/gear/anker-powercore-10000/) for phones.

Owners like the size, the alert and the flashlight. The main complaint is the lack of a disposable-battery backup. It is the small Midland pick in our [best hand crank radio](/best-hand-crank-radio/) roundup; for a battery backup, see the [Midland ER310](/gear/midland-er310/) or the [Eton FRX3+](/gear/eton-frx3-plus/).

faqs.q: Does the Midland ER210 take AA batteries?
faqs.a: No. It runs only on its built-in 2,600mAh lithium-ion pack, recharged by crank, solar or USB. That is the main trade-off against the larger ER310, which accepts six AA batteries as a backup. If you want a disposable-battery option in a compact radio, the Eton FRX3+ takes AAA batteries instead.

faqs.q: Can the Midland ER210 charge a phone?
faqs.a: Only as an emergency trickle, and maybe not at all. Midland’s FAQ warns that many newer iPhones and Android phones may not charge from it. Its 2,600mAh pack holds about 9.6Wh, less than one full phone charge even when it works. Keep a separate power bank for phones and save the radio’s pack for alerts.

verdict: The Kaito KA500 Voyager is the most radio in our roundup, for people who want shortwave and a proper reading lamp and do not mind the size.

**Shortwave is the niche extra.** Alongside AM, FM and seven NOAA weather channels with an alert mode, it adds two shortwave bands, which listings give as roughly 3.2–8 MHz and 9–22 MHz. Most households will never use shortwave, but it is one way to hear distant broadcasters if a regional disaster takes local stations off the air.

**The most flexible power options.** It runs from a hand crank, a solar panel that tilts to face the sun, USB, an AC adapter and three AA batteries. The tilt matters: a panel aimed at the sun produces noticeably more than one lying flat, the same rule that applies to folding panels like the [Goal Zero Nomad 20](/gear/goal-zero-nomad-20/). The AA backup works when crank and sun are not enough.

**Reading lamp, bigger body.** On the back of the solar panel is a 5-LED reading lamp that lights a table rather than a pinpoint, plus a standard flashlight. Retail listings put the radio at about 1.8 lb and 8 × 5 × 2.5 inches, the biggest here. Battery specs differ by version: listings describe a small Ni-MH pack in the standard model, and some variants add a larger lithium pack or a phone charger, so check the exact listing.

Owners like the reception, the shortwave and the reading lamp. The main complaints are the size and the small internal pack. It is the shortwave pick in our [best hand crank radio](/best-hand-crank-radio/) roundup; for a smaller alert radio, see the [Midland ER310](/gear/midland-er310/) or the [Eton FRX3+](/gear/eton-frx3-plus/).

faqs.q: Does the Kaito KA500 have a NOAA weather alert?
faqs.a: Yes. It receives seven NOAA weather channels and has an alert mode that sounds when a warning is broadcast on your local channel. Tune it to the strongest local channel and switch the alert mode on. Keep AA batteries installed or the internal pack charged during storm season so it can monitor overnight.

faqs.q: Do I need shortwave on an emergency radio?
faqs.a: Most households do not. AM, FM and NOAA weather radio cover local news and warnings. Shortwave, which the Kaito KA500 adds with two bands, lets you hear distant broadcasters if a regional disaster takes local stations off the air. It is a useful extra for rural areas and radio hobbyists, not a must-have.

verdict: The RunningSnail MD-090P is a good outage radio and phone top-up battery, but not a warning device, because it does not list an automatic NOAA alert.

**The biggest battery here.** RunningSnail's manual lists a 4,000mAh rechargeable battery, the largest among our picks. Some listings express it as 14,800mWh, which is the same pack described in energy: about 14.8Wh. That is close to one full charge for a typical phone after losses, far more than the 2,000–2,600mAh packs in most crank radios. It recharges by crank, solar or USB.

**Listen, but it will not wake you.** It receives AM, FM and all seven NOAA weather channels, so you can hear the forecast whenever you tune in. We could not find an automatic alert function listed for this model, so it will not sound a siren for a 3 a.m. tornado warning the way the [Midland ER310](/gear/midland-er310/) or [Eton FRX3+](/gear/eton-frx3-plus/) will. If you already have phone alerts or an alert radio, that is fine.

**A light that finds you.** Alongside a flashlight, it has a reading lamp with a motion sensor that switches on when you walk past in the dark, provided the switch is set to auto. That is handy in a hallway or a child's room during a long outage.

Owners like the large battery, the motion lamp and the price. The main complaints are thin documentation and listings that disagree on battery figures. RunningSnail sells several similar models, so confirm the model number. It is the biggest-battery pick in our [best hand crank radio](/best-hand-crank-radio/) roundup; for a dedicated phone bank, see the [Anker PowerCore 10000](/gear/anker-powercore-10000/).

verdict: The FosPower A1 is a sensible spare radio for a car or a second kit, as long as something else handles weather alerts.

**Crank, solar and AAA backup for little money.** Retail listings describe a 2,000mAh (7,400mWh) lithium-ion pack, recharged by hand crank, solar panel or micro-USB, plus a AAA battery compartment. That AAA backup keeps it useful when the internal pack is flat and the sky is grey. It receives AM, FM and the NOAA weather band from 162.400 to 162.550 MHz.

**No alert, small pack.** It does not list an automatic weather alert, so like the [RunningSnail MD-090P](/gear/runningsnail-md-090p/) it is a radio you listen to, not one that wakes you. The 7.4Wh pack gives only a modest phone top-up, less than half a charge for most phones after losses. Charge the pack before storm season, keep spare AAAs with it, and rely on a power bank such as the [Anker PowerCore 10000](/gear/anker-powercore-10000/) for phones.

**Built for a car kit.** It is small enough for a glovebox or day pack, and the IPX3 rating means it can handle splashes and light rain. The 1W flashlight is basic next to Midland's Cree LEDs, but it is enough to find a jack in a dark trunk.

Owners like the price and the AAA backup. The main complaint, as one owner put it, is that the crank is not enough to recharge other electronics, which matches what every maker in this category says. FosPower sells several similar models, so confirm the model number. It is the budget pick in our [best hand crank radio](/best-hand-crank-radio/) roundup; for alerts, see the [Midland ER310](/gear/midland-er310/).

verdict: The Eton Scorpion II is a rugged, compact crank radio built to clip onto a pack, a bike or a boat. It is a good outdoor and car-kit radio, but like the FosPower A1 it is a radio you listen to, not one that wakes you for warnings.

**Built for knocking around.** Eton designs it as a rugged, splash-resistant radio with a built-in carabiner and a bottle opener, so it hangs from a pack strap or a tent loop. It is small enough for a glovebox or a kayak hatch.

**Three ways to charge.** A built-in rechargeable pack takes power from the hand crank, a solar panel on top or USB. It receives AM, FM and the NOAA weather band, so you can listen to forecasts and emergency broadcasts. We could not find an automatic NOAA alert listed for this model, so for overnight warnings pair it with an alert radio like the [Midland ER310](/gear/midland-er310/) or the [Eton FRX3+](/gear/eton-frx3-plus/), or rely on phone alerts.

Treat that as a trickle: cranking makes very little power, and a dedicated bank like the [Anker PowerCore 10000](/gear/anker-powercore-10000/) holds far more.
